title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (7 of 7)
hook: the face of truth covered with gold
carry: uncover it, so I may see
tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (1 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, vidya: know both together, knowing and doing, vidya and avidya. Either alone goes dark.

Some things that get in the way of seeing clearly are ugly. But the hardest ones to see past are beautiful. A great job that's slowly emptying you. Praise that feels so good you stop asking whether it's deserved. A shiny screen at midnight. The Isha ends with a picture of exactly this. Not truth hidden behind a wall, or a curtain, or a mess. Truth hidden behind gold. And then the text does something it hasn't done all week. It prays.
screen: `THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS IN THE WAY.` → `NOT A WALL.` → `GOLD.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen: hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc, or a golden vessel, like a lid. The speaker turns to Pushan, the nourisher, a name for the sun: uncover it, so that I, whose way is truth, may see. Verse sixteen goes on: spread out your rays, gather in your light, so I can see your most blessed form. Then a startling line: that person there, I am he. The one hidden behind the gold is not a stranger. Verse seventeen is spoken at the edge of death: the breath goes back to the immortal wind, and this body ends in ashes. Then: om, mind, remember. Remember what was done. And verse eighteen, the last, turns to Agni, fire: lead us by the good path, you who know all our ways; take away from us the crooked wrong. Tradition gives these verses a place at deathbeds and funerals, and they read that way: close, and quiet. They aren't a new teaching. They're the whole week turned into a prayer. So, the week. All this is pervaded by the Lord. By that renounced, enjoy. Keep working a hundred years, and the work won't cling. It moves and doesn't move, far and near. See the self in all beings and stop shrinking back. Hold knowing and doing together. And when even the good things shine too brightly, ask for the gold to be moved aside. Eighteen verses, isha: nothing here is only mine.
screen: `THE FACE OF TRUTH, COVERED WITH GOLD.` · `UNCOVER IT, SO I MAY SEE.` · `MIND, REMEMBER.` · `LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.` · then, large: `ISHA.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what the golden lid in your life is right now: something good, even lovely, that might be keeping you from seeing what's true; you don't have to remove it, just name it quietly. Then breathe, and on each out-breath imagine the lid lifting a little. If you pray, you can say the verse's own request in your own language, uncover it, so I may see; otherwise, just watch the breath.
Hiranmaya, golden, made of gold. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc; Pushan, the sun, is asked to uncover it, so the truthful may see.
Your line: uncover it, so I may see. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad that starts with a child's question. That's the whole Isha, and day two hundred thirty-eight.

screen: `DAY 238 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KENA UPANISHAD, WHO IMPELS THE MIND?`

howItsDone: Isha verses 15–18 are recited at some Hindu funerals and at the bedside of the dying; verse 18, the prayer to Agni to lead by the good path, also appears in the Rig Veda (1.189.1).

original.note: Sanskrit: hiranmaya, golden, made of gold; verse 15: the face of truth covered with a golden disc.

trapdoor: what you thought: what hides the truth must be something bad.
what it means: in the Isha, the lid over truth is golden, beautiful things can blind too.
what a scholar hears: hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham also appears, with small variations, in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (5.15).
